column3: Repeats the settlement elites' collective rejection of what warners are sent with.
Frames the messenger's task as truthful descent joined to warning, the office rejected in the focus.
Shows a detailed book arriving as guidance, supplying the kind of warrant absent from ancestral imitation.
Parallels a powerful group's rejection of what others have accepted.
Directly asks whether the community possesses a prior book to hold onto.
Shows rejecting hearers dismissing a presented sign and its bearers rather than testing it.
Repeats the formula of rejecting what messengers were sent with, despite an alternative objection.
Supplies the immediately preceding pattern: elites cite ancestral practice when a warner arrives.
Contrasts hypothetical claims of better guidance with conduct once clear guidance actually arrives.
States the inherited-guidance claim that 43:24 challenges.
Extends the focus's appeal to earlier messengers by questioning their worship precedent.
Offers a criterion for following rightly guided messengers, without addressing inherited practice.
Direct parallel: revelation is declined in favor of ancestral following, whose guidance is questioned.
Generalizes the recurring placement of a warner in each settlement.
Names human ingratitude or rejection but adds no ancestral or messenger scene.
Directly contrasts divine and messenger guidance with sufficiency of ancestral practice.
Provides the immediate narrative consequence for the deniers in the focus's recurring pattern.
An accusation of enormity does not clarify guidance, ancestry, or the messenger's proposal.
Shows a messenger pressing whether a clear thing brought should alter the response.
Locates the arrival of truth and a clear messenger within the same ancestral setting.
A future disbelievers' cry does not illuminate the focus's present exchange.
Direct parallel: divine guidance is refused for what was found upon the fathers, even under a warning.
Presents Abraham's confidence in future guidance but not the contested inherited track.
Witnessing among communities is not materially connected to the focus's dispute.
Historical messengers bring clear proofs and are explicitly rejected for what they were sent with.
Clarifies the messenger's paired role as bearer of good news and warning.
Uses disbelief in a different contrast about hope.
Shows truth being met with deflection, comparison, and comprehensive rejection.
Begins a later in-surah instance of a messenger sent with signs to an established elite.
A community's accusation in a distinct episode adds no relevant guidance pattern.
Shows ancestral custom invoked to justify conduct, then challenged as unsupported knowledge.
Identifies a warner addressing his people but lacks the focus's dispute.
The ritual critique does not clarify ancestral guidance or the offered better way.
Combines a claim to speak only truth with the arrival of a clear proof through Moses.
Establishes the repeated sending of prophets among earlier peoples.
Contrasts bringing truth with its confirmation, an alternative to preemptive rejection.
Shows selective acceptance of inherited revelation while rejecting confirming truth beyond it.
Clarifies the modest office of a clear warner.
Shows disbelievers crowding before the messenger without resolving their response to guidance.
A messenger brings clear proofs and wisdom to clarify disputed matters, matching the focus's offer of better direction.
Makes prior deniers an example for later people, without explaining the inherited claim.
Describes persistent disbelief as a settled refusal of faith.
A final confirmation of promises has no direct bearing on the exchange.
Links opposition to God and messenger with clear signs and prior historical precedents.
Moses' clear proofs meet arrogance, paralleling refusal despite evidence.
Mentions fathers only as a comparison for remembrance, not as an authority claim.
Continues the surah's challenge to measuring truth by wealth and status.
Shows clear proofs followed by a contrary attachment, illustrating that evidence can be refused.
Separates allegiance to fathers from faith when they prefer disbelief.
States divine descent but adds no reception or ancestral contrast.
A disputed matter arriving for Lot is not a guidance-versus-ancestry scene.
Questions powerless intercessors but does not address the focus's response to a messenger.
Shows a conditional claim of guidance in Pharaoh's crisis, a different form of response.
Affirms divine guidance and protection without the social dispute in the focus.
A messenger arrives with signs and thereby exemplifies an offered evidentiary guidance.
Hidden reverence and fear of the Hour do not clarify the focus.
The returning heart is not connected to rejecting an incoming messenger.
Contrasts a prophet's departure from an unbelieving community with the focus's ancestral defense.
Provides the later in-surah response of forbearance after their rejection.
Joins faith in and following the messenger with hoped-for guidance.
Forgetting part of a reminder concerns covenant failure rather than ancestral imitation.
States the ancestral basis for continuing idolatrous worship.
Shows people rejecting the very reminder they had demanded.
Legal instruction and guidance are too remote from the focus's exchange.
Addresses the same surah's status-based assumptions about who may receive divine mercy.
Defines guided security but does not engage the competing ancestral route.
A teaching on charity and showmanship does not add to the focus.
States that the messenger is only a clear warner, relevant to the rejected commission.
A sound heart in Abraham's story is too indirect.
The messenger's lack of refuge outside God does not explain the focus's refusal.
A later scene of punishment does not clarify the offered better guidance.
Rules for witnesses in accusation are unrelated to the focus.
Attributes guidance to God, grounding the focus's claim of a more guiding way.
A warning's eventual recognition has only a general relation to rejecting warners.
Pairs disbelief with blocking God's way, clarifying the practical direction of rejection.
Shows a messenger completing delivery and counsel before separating from a disbelieving people.
Supplies the immediate prior unsupported claim used to preserve their inherited worship.
Rejection of God and messenger explains failed offerings but not the ancestral argument.
Directly portrays hearers accusing incoming messengers of turning them from their fathers' way.
Restricts intercession to truthful knowing testimony, only indirectly relevant.
Links rejection of divine signs to not being guided, matching the refusal of better guidance.
Later in the surah, the same people label arriving truth and reject it.
A judgment against obstinate disbelief adds no interpretive detail to the exchange.
Questions communal fixation on inherited worship, opening the challenge made explicit in the focus.
Hypocritical testimony is a distinct speech problem from ancestral refusal.
Explicitly diagnoses both the people and their fathers as being in manifest error.
Presents guidance to the Lord as the messenger's offer, though without ancestral comparison.
States ancestral practice as the sole answer to a challenge over worship.
A different messenger visit and announced destruction do not clarify the focus.
Future regret of the disbeliever does not add to the ancestral-guidance dispute.
A question about forefathers in resurrection denial is only a lexical parallel.
Juxtaposes guidance with rejection of divine signs, supporting the stakes of the focus's refusal.
Mutual waiting supplies no guidance or ancestry connection.
Defines a category of disbelief without the focus's selective social rationale.
Shows a group dismissing believers as foolish rather than reconsidering its stance.
The punishment statement does not clarify the immediate interpretive exchange.
Normalizes the succession of earlier messengers and signs by divine permission.
Sets out guidance as given while leaving the response open between gratitude and rejection.
The image of raised dust has no relevant connection.
A recompense for Noah's rejected servant is too remote from the focus's dispute.
Directly records a people resisting a messenger because he calls them to leave what their fathers worshiped.
Preserves the contrary ancestral appeal that later generations inherit association from their fathers.
Directly voices resistance to a prophet because his call would require leaving ancestral worship.
Directly frames prophetic guidance as a threat to what the fathers worshiped.
Shows associators invoking both divine will and ancestral practice to avoid a messenger's demand.
Denies that people or their fathers possess knowledge for an inherited theological assertion.
Abraham challenges his father's inherited worship by asking why he serves what neither hears nor helps.
Portrays leaders rejecting a human messenger and appealing to what was known among their forefathers.
Makes the ancestral objects of worship explicit within Abraham's challenge to inherited practice.
Directly casts the messenger as one accused of turning people away from what their fathers worshiped.
Describes people finding their fathers astray and then hastening along their tracks.
Shows opponents rejecting a call as unprecedented because they did not hear it in an inherited religious setting.
Shows communities meeting messengers' clear proofs with a self-satisfied prior knowledge rather than reception.
Adds that every prophet sent among the earlier peoples was met with mockery, extending the focus's recurring pattern.
Counters the assumption that the messenger's call is unprecedented by locating him within prior messengers.
Has condemned hearers admit that a warner came and that they nevertheless denied him.
